newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanese detect swing in U.S. policy.
newsitem.headline: Lebanese detect swing in U.S. policy.

text.p: The Washington donors conference that pledged $3.2 billion to Lebanon's reconstruction signalled an important change in the attitude of the United States and the world community toward the Middle Eastern country, Beirut analysts said on Tuesday.

Commentators were ecstatic that Monday's U.S.-sponsored gathering of some 30 countries and eight international financial institutions pledged more than $1 billion in immediate official aid and $2.2 billion in longterm programmes.
"We need to rub our eyes and pinch ourselves to make sure this is not a dream," wrote columnist Elias ad-Deiri Zayan in the conservative Beirut newspaper an-Nahar.

Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri had asked the "Friends of Lebanon" conference for $5 billion over five years to carry on post-civil war reconstruction, but Lebanese officials had played down the possibility of achieving that sum.
A Beirut banker, asked to comment on the result, cautiously recalled that previous donor conferences had pledged large sums for Lebanon's reconstruction that did not materialise.
"What is this long-term $2.2 billion?" he said, preferring to await details of the pledges before commenting.
But more than the money, politicians expressed delight at the attention Lebanon was getting after being sidelined during and after its 1975-90 civil war.
"It's great for such a small country to be the focus of international attention," President Elias Hrawi was quoted as saying.

"It's enough comfort for me to see this large number of important countries gathering in Washington itself and under Secretary of State Warren Christopher...to discuss aid to Lebanon in its effort to build its future," Hrawi told an-Nahar.
An-Nahar said the conference resulted in an "international declaration of intent to return Lebanon to the world political map.
"This signifies a shift in America's attitude towards Lebanon, and possible signs of a change in its policy towards the (Middle East) peace process," the newspaper said.

Analysts consoled themselves over Washington's failure to announce a hoped-for easing of its 11-year-old travel ban on Lebanon by noting that U.S. officials said the issue was being actively reviewed and a decision could be taken soon.

"By the way U.S. officials spoke about it there is still a chance that it will be lifted before Christopher leaves office," Michael Young, editor of the Beirut political review The Lebanon Report, told Reuters. Christopher's term ends on January 20.
Young said the conference and its results should be seen "in the light of a change of heart taking place in Washington" that was affecting its perception of Lebanon.

Washington has for years left Lebanon under Syrian tutelage, virtually ignoring it while encouraging Syria to negotiate peace with Israel. But the Syria-Israel peace process is now blocked and Young said the United States considered the policy had failed.
"The Friends of Lebanon conference is an effort to open the door a bit to another possibility, to reaffirm Lebanon as an actor," Young said.
"By strengthening Lebanon's economy, you are loosening Syria's hold on Lebanon," he said.

Any weakening of Syria's position in Lebanon -- by economic, political or military means -- would help reduce the pressure on Israel to make territorial concessions to Syria on the Golan Heights, he added.
